One_Body_Too_Many: One Body Too Many is a 1944 American comedy horror mystery film directed by Frank McDonald, starring Bela Lugosi, Jack Haley and Lyle Talbot. The film was the second comedy featuring Haley to be produced by Pine-Thomas Productions, part of the studio's new direction towards comedy films. The original intention was to hire Boris Karloff for the film's key horror role, but Lugosi was hired instead.

rv: An eccentric millionaire's unread will, and a mansion full of contentious heirs. What better time for a life insurance salesman to show up, especially if he's played by Jack "Tin Man" Haley. Toss in a wandering corpse and butler Bela Lugosi constantly trying to serve everybody rat-poison-laced coffee, and you have the fixins for a comic who-done-it in the old dark house mold. All we need is a thunderstorm. Aha! There it is now! Jean Parker is the damsel in peril. The ubiquitous Lyle Talbot is on hand in a supporting role. This one is fun. CAST NOTE: Either as a leading man or character actor…

A fun comedy mystery. I like Bela Lugosi movies. They tend to be strange in an entertaining way.
Jack Haley proves he's a good comedic lead in this "old dark house" movie. Lugosi, unfortunately, has a small role but he makes the most of it with a running joke throughout the movie.

rv: Lovely MOS scenic footage highlights this short, along with the bubbly narration of Art Gilmore. Plenty of shots of diesel-engine Santa Fe trains and a few nice shots of 19th century steam locomotives. The film is a well-written commercial with a little sub-plot about two children (the boy is wearing a suit and bow tie) on a thousand-mile trip. Railroads pay taxes, you know. As if other businesses don't, Editing is plentiful to hold interest and sound effects are well-chosen. A fine Dudley production. Oh, and there's plenty of flag-waving at the beginning and end. America's the greatest, you…

At 6:25 mark, workers with possible dirty hands are loading UNWRAPPED raw meat meant for human consumption. Appears meat was cross contaminated in an unrefrigerated box? My goodness, back in the days before plastic gloves and health codes. What was with the ending: "Railroads pay taxes for schools?" Most scenes appeared to be college footage, not public schools. Propaganda, silly script, and bad graphics places this up there with the classic "Duck & Cover." Thanks to the person who saved this treasure.

There was a period after WW2 when both the left and the right pushed the self-congratulatory concept of the U.S. being a unity of races and creeds. Trade unions pushed it in "Brotherhood of Man." Corporate America promoted it in films produced by John Sutherland. Even Jack Benny gave speeches at the end of his radio show about how the Nazis tried to "weaken America" by causing racial and religious divisions. This Coronet film does the same thing, harping on the message that people came from everywhere to settle the U.S. and they've "mixed." (The film bypasses the human population already on…

If you're the old-fashioned type, you may enjoy this encapsulation of the orthodox "America as melting pot" story. If you're a cynic, you'll find this a saccharine piece of propaganda that ignores the real answer to it's question: Native Americans (aside from the predictable mention of corn). If you're a film buff, you may admire the editing, but find the narration a bore. But if you need loads of stock footage of people in various states of work and play in the early 1950's, you're in luck.
